name: Triceps extension
angleNote: Elbow flexion: 0° = arm straight (end of the lift), 140° = fully bent (start). Lifting makes the angle smaller.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The forearm segment includes the hand (combined centre of mass along elbow → grip).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Shoulder→elbow and elbow→grip centre in metres, typical adult.

strengthCurve.label: Elbow extensor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric elbow-extension torque vs elbow flexion (0° = straight), peak about 55°: the paper's mean cubic fit, normalised, inside the measured 20–116° (held flat beyond). Measured with the upper arm raised 90° to the side, so the long head's length differs from overhead or arm-at-side positions. Peak torque default: the paper's mean over all participants (58 Nm; men 77 Nm, women 36 Nm). Variants correct for the shoulder angle with Guenzkofer et al.'s measurements, relative to the arm at the side.
strengthCurve.source: Pinter IJ, Bobbert MF, van Soest AJ, Smeets JBJ (2010). Isometric torque–angle relationships of the elbow flexors and extensors in the transverse plane. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 20:923–931. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2010.05.001

muscles.name: Triceps (long head)
muscles.note: Crosses the shoulder too, so it is stretched (and in reality stronger) with the arm overhead. The model can't show that: weights depend on the elbow angle only.

muscles.name: Triceps (lateral and medial heads)
muscles.note: Cross the elbow only, so they work much the same in every variant.

muscles.name: Anconeus
muscles.note: Small muscle behind the elbow that assists extension near lockout.

phases.name: Lockout
phases.text: Arm nearly straight. Triceps are weakest here; what the load does depends entirely on its direction.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: Forearm across the line of pull: free weights have their largest moment arm here.

phases.name: Stretched
phases.text: Elbow fully bent. Overhead and lying versions still load this position; a pushdown mostly does not.

variants.name: Cable pushdown
variants.notes: Upper arm by your side, cable from a high pulley. The pull is almost straight up, so the torque peaks with the forearm horizontal and fades at the bottom. The forearm's own weight helps you here.

strengthScale.note: arm at the side: the reference posture for the other variants' corrections (Guenzkofer et al., shoulder at 0°).
strengthScale.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric)

variants.name: Overhead dumbbell extension
variants.notes: Upper arm pointing up. Torque = m·g·L·sin(elbow angle), largest with the forearm horizontal behind the head. The long head is stretched in this position, which this model can't credit.

strengthScale.note: arm overhead: elbow-extension strength 85–90% of arm-at-side. Guenzkofer et al. measured it at 135° of shoulder flexion (the highest they tested; held there for 180°). Despite the long head being stretched overhead, the measured torque was lower, not higher.
strengthScale.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric)

variants.name: Lying EZ-bar extension (skullcrusher)
variants.notes: Lying on your back with the upper arm vertical. Relative to gravity this is the overhead extension turned through 90°, so the torque curve is identical. Load is per arm (half the bar).

strengthScale.note: upper arm at 90° of shoulder flexion: 89–95% of arm-at-side, interpolated between Guenzkofer et al.'s 60° and 135°.
strengthScale.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric)
